title: World History: The Big Picture · Episode 2

units.t: World History: The Big Picture. Episode two.
In this episode: The printing press changed everything, The Renaissance and The Industrial Revolution.
Part one. The printing press changed everything.
One goldsmith's invention sparked religious revolutions, modern science and, eventually, the idea of news.
From scribes to type.
Before the mid-1400s, European books were copied by hand, often by monks.
One Bible could take a scribe over a year, copying introduced errors, and a library of a few hundred volumes was a treasure.
Most people never owned a book, and most couldn't read.
Knowledge sat in churches, universities and wealthy homes.
Around 1440, Mainz goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg developed printing with movable metal type.
He cast individual letters in a hand mould so they could be arranged into pages, inked, printed and reused.
He adapted the screw press used for wine and olive oil and developed an oil-based ink that stuck to metal.
His Bible, printed around 1455, is still considered one of the most beautiful books ever made.
About 49 copies survive.
Not the first.
Printing wasn't new everywhere.
China had woodblock printing centuries earlier; the Diamond Sutra, printed in 868, is the oldest dated printed book.
Around 1040, Bi Sheng invented movable type from baked clay.
Korea was printing with movable metal type by the 1200s, and its Jikji of 1377 is the oldest surviving book printed that way, decades before Gutenberg.
But Chinese writing uses thousands of characters, which made movable type harder to use.
Gutenberg's system suited Europe's small alphabet, and combined with a trading economy hungry for books, it spread explosively.
An information explosion.
By 1500, presses were running in more than 200 European towns, and historians estimate millions of books had been printed.
Prices fell dramatically, so merchants, lawyers and craftspeople could afford books.
Ideas that once took years to spread by hand could travel the continent in months, in identical copies.
Mistakes could be corrected in the next edition rather than multiplied by tired copyists.
In 1517, German monk Martin Luther wrote his 95 Theses criticising the Catholic Church's sale of indulgences.
Thanks to print, his writings spread across Germany quickly, and he became one of the best-selling authors of his time.
He translated the Bible into German so ordinary people could read it.
The resulting Protestant Reformation split Western Christianity and reshaped Europe for centuries.
Science and literacy.
Science depends on sharing results so others can check and build on them.
Printed books and, later, journals made this possible at scale.
Accurate diagrams, maps and tables could be copied exactly, which hand copying never managed.
Copernicus's book arguing that the Earth orbits the Sun was printed in 1543, followed by Galileo, Kepler and Newton.
The first scientific journals appeared in 1665.
As books got cheaper, more people learned to read.
Printers needed consistent spelling and grammar, which helped standardise languages like English and German.
Pamphlets, and eventually newspapers from the early 1600s, created a public sphere where ordinary people could debate current events.
Governments and churches saw the danger, and censorship followed.
The internet, 500 years later.
Historians often compare the printing press with the internet.
Both made publishing dramatically cheaper and faster.
Both spread knowledge, but also propaganda, scandal and misinformation; early printers churned out sensational pamphlets about witches and monsters.
Both shifted power away from traditional gatekeepers and provoked anxious debates about information overload.
It took societies generations to develop norms, like editors, libraries and reputable publishers, to cope with print.
We're still working out the equivalent for the internet.
The key idea: Gutenberg's press, with reusable movable metal type, replaced slow hand copying around 1440.
Part two. The Renaissance.
How a handful of Italian cities rediscovered the ancient world and reinvented art, science and what it means to be human.
Rebirth in Italy.
The Renaissance, French for 'rebirth', was a cultural revival in Europe from roughly the 14th to the 17th century.
It began in Italy, especially Florence, and spread to France, the Netherlands, Germany and England.
People then felt they were reviving ancient Greece and Rome after a long decline.
Historians now see the 'Dark Ages' as less dark than Renaissance writers claimed.
Italy had advantages.
Cities such as Florence, Venice and Milan grew rich on trade, banking and manufacturing.
Roman ruins were everywhere.
Competing city-states used art and architecture to show off their power.
And after Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453, Greek scholars fled to Italy with ancient manuscripts.
Humanism and patrons.
Scholars hunted through monastery libraries for lost Greek and Roman writing on philosophy, history, science and poetry.
This inspired humanism, an outlook celebrating human potential, reason and achievement alongside religious devotion.
Humanists believed a well-rounded education in grammar, rhetoric, history and moral philosophy made better citizens.
The poet Petrarch, often called its father, helped launch it in the 1300s.
Our 'humanities' come from it.
Art needed money, and the Renaissance ran on patronage.
The Medici of Florence, bankers, paid artists, architects and scholars for generations.
Popes commissioned huge projects, including rebuilding St Peter's Basilica.
Guilds and merchants funded church decorations to display piety and status.
Fierce competition for commissions pushed standards higher.
Art gets real.
Around 1415, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, a mathematical way of creating the illusion of depth on a flat surface, with lines converging on a vanishing point.
Painters quickly adopted it.
Artists also studied anatomy, sometimes by dissecting corpses, to paint realistic bodies, and used light and shadow to create volume.
Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.
Michelangelo sculpted David and painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
Raphael painted The School of Athens.
The Renaissance person.
Leonardo da Vinci was a painter, engineer, anatomist, inventor and scientist.
His notebooks, written in mirror script, hold designs for flying machines, armoured vehicles and diving suits, along with remarkably accurate anatomical drawings.
He embodies the 'Renaissance man': someone skilled across many fields.
The ideal was a cultivated person who could discuss art, science, poetry and politics, not specialise in one thing.
The same curiosity reached practical fields.
In 1494 Luca Pacioli, a friend of Leonardo, published the first printed explanation of double-entry bookkeeping, still the basis of accounting today.
Exploration and legacy.
The Renaissance spirit of questioning and observation spilled into exploration.
Mapmakers constantly redrew the world as new reports arrived, and European navigators sailed to the Americas, around Africa and across the Pacific.
These voyages brought wealth and knowledge to Europe, but also colonisation, conquest and devastating consequences for Indigenous peoples.
The printing press, arriving in the mid-1400s, spread Renaissance ideas quickly, as books and engravings reached readers across Europe.
The period laid foundations for the Scientific Revolution, the Enlightenment and modern ideas about education and individual achievement.
You can see its influence in old European cities, and in grand Australian public buildings with columns and domes.
The key idea: The Renaissance was a revival of ancient learning and art that began in Italy's wealthy, competing city-states.
Part three. The Industrial Revolution.
For most of history, almost everyone was a farmer.
Then, in about a century, machines changed everything.
Why Britain first.
For thousands of years most people worked the land, and living standards barely changed from one century to the next.
From around 1760 in Britain, that began to change.
Machines powered first by water, then by coal-fired steam, replaced hand tools.
Production moved from homes into factories.
Historians often call it the most important change in human life since farming.
Britain had a combination of advantages: plentiful coal and iron ore, often close together; banks and investors willing to fund new ventures; relatively stable politics; and a large trading empire.
High wages and cheap coal made labour-saving machines especially worth inventing.
Much of the cotton came from plantations worked by enslaved people in the Americas, a dark foundation of the new wealth.
Cotton and the factory.
The revolution began in textiles.
Inventions like James Hargreaves' spinning jenny, around 1764, and Richard Arkwright's water frame let one worker spin many threads at once.
Arkwright's mill at Cromford, opened in 1771, is often called the first modern factory, with workers arriving for set shifts to tend machines.
Output soared and cloth became cheap.
For workers, it meant long hours, strict discipline and dangerous machinery.
The factory changed how people spent their days as much as what they produced.
Iron, coal and rails.
Traditional ironmaking needed charcoal, and Britain's woodlands were running short.
In 1709 Abraham Darby at Coalbrookdale in Shropshire smelted iron with coke, coal baked to drive off impurities.
With coal abundant, iron could be made far more cheaply.
In 1779 his grandson built the first major cast-iron bridge over the River Severn nearby.
It still stands and gave Ironbridge its name.
Cheap iron went into engines, machinery, rails and ships.
The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in 1825.
The Liverpool and Manchester Railway in 1830 was the first to run regular passenger services entirely by steam.
Journeys that took days by horse took hours.
Railways even standardised time, because timetables demanded one national time instead of each town's own.
City life and progress.
People poured from the countryside into cities like Manchester, which grew from a market town into one of the world's first industrial cities.
Housing was cramped and poorly built, and cholera spread through contaminated water.
Children as young as five or six worked in mills and mines.
Reformers pushed back: Britain's Factory Acts from 1833 limited child labour, public health laws brought sewers and clean water, and unions fought for better wages and shorter hours.
Historians debate how quickly ordinary people benefited.
For the first generations, wages rose slowly and life expectancy in industrial towns was low.
Over the long run, the gains were enormous: goods became cheaper and incomes rose many times over.
Much of the rise in living standards since 1800 followed from the technologies that began in those British mills.
The long shadow.
The Industrial Revolution created the modern world: factories, cities, mass-produced goods, railways, the middle class, and eventually electricity, cars and computers.
It also began the large-scale burning of coal, then oil and gas.
Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has risen from about 280 parts per million before industrialisation to over 420 today, driving climate change.
The same engine that lifted living standards carries a cost we are still paying.
Many argue we are now living through the next great transition, from fossil fuels to clean energy.
The key idea: From about 1760, Britain's coal, capital, colonies and high wages made it the birthplace of machine-powered industry.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What made Gutenberg's system practical for printing many pages?
Answer. Reusable metal letters arranged into pages.
Question two. What helped make Italy the birthplace of the Renaissance?
Answer. Trade wealth, Roman ruins and competing city-states.
Question three. Why was Britain well placed to start the Industrial Revolution?
Answer. Plentiful coal, willing investors, trade and high wages.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
